title_en: Shimano Co., Ltd. v. Ningbo Richeng Industry and Trade Co., Ltd. — patent infringement dispute
ruling_gist_en: A use environment feature that has been written into a claim is an essential technical feature and has a limiting effect on the scope of protection of the claim. full_text_en:
Shimano Co., Ltd. v. Ningbo Richen Industry & Trade Co., Ltd. — patent infringement dispute

【Ruling Summary】

A use environment feature that has been written into a claim is an essential technical feature and serves to define the scope of protection of the claim. The degree to which a use environment feature defines the scope of protection of a claim shall be specifically determined on a case-by-case basis. Generally, it should be understood that it is sufficient for the subject matter sought to be protected to be usable in that use environment, and it is not required that the subject matter sought to be protected must be used in that use environment; however, this does not apply where a person of ordinary skill in the art can clearly and reasonably ascertain, after reading the patent claims, specification, and patent examination file, that the subject matter sought to be protected must be used in that use environment.

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court

(2012) Civil Retrial No. 1

Petitioner for Retrial (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance, Original Petitioner for Retrial): Shimano Co., Ltd. Address: 77 San-chome, Oimatsu-cho, Sakai-ku, Sakai City, Osaka Prefecture, Japan.

Legal Representative: Shimano Yozo, Chairman of the Board.

Agent ad litem: Dong Wei, attorney at Beijing Puhua Law Firm.

Agent ad litem: Wang Ying, intern attorney at Beijing Puhua Law Firm.

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance, Original Respondent): Ningbo Richen Industry & Trade Co., Ltd. Address: Shengshan Town Industrial Development Zone, Cixi City, Zhejiang Province, People's Republic of China.

Legal Representative: Xu Mingqiang, General Manager.

Agent ad litem: Yu Jikun, Deputy General Manager of Ningbo Richen Industry & Trade Co., Ltd.

Agent ad litem: Dai Xiaoxiang, attorney at Zhejiang Xiaoxiang Law Firm.

With respect to the dispute over infringement of invention patent between the Petitioner for Retrial, Shimano Co., Ltd., and the Respondent, Ningbo Richen Industry & Trade Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Richen Company), the Petitioner for Retrial, Shimano Co., Ltd., being dissatisfied with the Civil Judgment (2009) Zhe Min Zai Zi No. 135 rendered by the Zhejiang High People's Court of the People's Republic of China, applied to this Court for retrial. This Court, by Civil Ruling (2011) Min Jian Zi No. 151 dated December 9, 2011, decided to initiate a retrial of this case. This Court lawfully formed a collegial panel and held a public hearing of this case on March 6, 2012. Dong Wei and Wang Ying, agents ad litem of Shimano Co., Ltd., and Yu Jikun and Dai Xiaoxiang, agents ad litem of Richen Company, appeared before the court to participate in the proceedings. The trial of this case has now concluded.

On August 27, 2004, Shimano Co., Ltd. filed a lawsuit with the Ningbo Intermediate People's Court of Zhejiang Province, alleging that it was the patentee of Invention Patent No. ZL94102612.4. Starting from 2003, it had discovered in the mainland Chinese market that bicycle rear derailleurs of models RD-HG-30A and RD-HG-40A manufactured and sold by Richen Company infringed upon the above patent rights of Shimano Co., Ltd. It requested the People's Court to order: 1. that Richen Company immediately cease manufacturing and selling the infringing products; 2. that Richen Company immediately destroy all remaining infringing products, promotional materials for the infringing products, and special molds used for manufacturing the infringing products, and remove advertisements for the infringing products from the internet; and 3. that Richen Company compensate Shimano Co., Ltd. for economic losses of RMB 300,000.

Richen Company defended, arguing that during the patent examination process, Shimano Co., Ltd. had repeatedly amended the claims at the request of the Patent Office to obtain the patent, the most clear of which was the addition of the technical feature "the connection structure of the rear fork end extension of the bicycle frame." This added technical feature indicated that in the technical solution of Shimano Co., Ltd.'s invention patent, the rear fork end of the bicycle frame must be provided with an extension, the extension must be provided with a dedicated connection structure, and that connection structure was used to install a derailleur. Therefore, the patent protected an improved rear fork end of the frame, a rear derailleur, and an assembly plan therefor. The accused infringing product did not involve a bicycle frame at all; it could be assembled on various types and structures of conventional bicycles, and thus the accused infringing product did not fall within the scope of protection of the patent.

After trial, the court of first instance found that Shimano Co., Ltd. was the patentee of Chinese Invention Patent No. ZL94102612.4, titled "Rear Derailleur Bracket" (hereinafter referred to as the patent-in-suit). The patent application date was February 3, 1994, and the date of grant announcement was December 11, 2002. The patent remains valid and is protected by law. The claims of the granted patent-in-suit state: "1. A bicycle rear derailleur bracket for connecting a rear derailleur (100) to a bicycle frame (50), the rear derailleur having a bracket member (5), a support member (4) for supporting a chain guide device (3), and a pair of connecting members (6, 7) for connecting the support member (4) and the bracket member (5), the bicycle frame having a connection structure (14a) formed on a derailleur mounting extension (14) of a rear fork end (51) of the bicycle frame, the rear derailleur bracket comprising: a bracket body (8) formed of a substantially L-shaped plate; a first connection structure (8a) provided near one end of the bracket body (8) for connecting the bracket member (5) of the rear derailleur (100) to the bracket body (8) so as to be pivotable about a first axis (91); a second connection structure (8b) provided near the other end of the bracket body (8) for connecting the bracket body (8) to the connection structure (14a) of the bicycle frame (50); and a positioning structure (8c) for contacting the derailleur mounting extension (14) so as to position the rear derailleur (100) relative to the rear fork end (51) at a predetermined orientation; characterized in that: the first connection structure (8a) and the second connection structure (8b) are arranged such that, when the bracket body (8) is mounted on the rear fork end (51), a connection point provided by the first connection structure (8a) is below and behind a connection point provided by the second connection structure (8b). 2. The bicycle rear derailleur bracket according to claim 1, characterized in that the second connection structure (8b) is in the form of a substantially circular hole. 3. The bicycle rear derailleur bracket according to claim 2, characterized in that it has a connecting bolt (16) passing through the substantially circular hole and tightened to connect the bracket body and the rear derailleur mounting extension (14) to each other. 4. The bicycle rear derailleur bracket according to claim 1, characterized in that the positioning structure (8c) is located adjacent to the second connection structure (8b). 5. The bicycle rear derailleur bracket according to claim 2, characterized in that the positioning structure (8c) is a protrusion extending from the surface of the plate. 6. The bicycle rear derailleur bracket according to claim 5, characterized in that the positioning structure (8c) is formed by pressing."

During the examination process of the patent-in-suit, the content of claim 1 in the original text submitted by Shimano Co., Ltd. was: "1. A rear derailleur bracket for connecting a rear derailleur to a bicycle frame on a connection structure formed on a derailleur mounting extension of a rear fork end of a bicycle frame, the rear derailleur bracket comprising: a bracket body; a first connection structure provided near one end of the bracket body for connecting the rear derailleur to the bracket body; a second connection structure provided near the other end of the bracket body for connecting the bracket body to the connection structure of the bicycle frame; and a positioning structure for contacting the derailleur mounting extension so as to position the rear derailleur relative to the rear fork end at a predetermined orientation." The State Patent Office of the People's Republic of China (later renamed the State Intellectual Property Office), in its first Office Action, considered that the prior art had already disclosed a bicycle rear derailleur mounting bracket for mounting a bicycle rear derailleur to a rear fork end of a bicycle frame, and that the technical solution defined in claim 1 lacked novelty with respect to the prior art disclosed in the cited document. Thereafter, Shimano Co., Ltd. amended claim 1 of the patent-in-suit to the following: "1. A rear derailleur bracket for connecting a rear derailleur (100) to a bicycle frame (50), the bicycle frame having a connection structure (14a) formed on a derailleur mounting extension (14) of a rear fork end (51) of the bicycle frame, the rear derailleur bracket comprising: a bracket body (8); a first connection structure (8a) provided near one end of the bracket body (8) for connecting the rear derailleur (100) to the bracket body (8); a second connection structure (8b) provided near the other end of the bracket body (8) for connecting the bracket body (8) to the connection structure (14a) of the bicycle frame (50); and a positioning structure (8c) for contacting the derailleur mounting extension (14) so as to position the rear derailleur (100) relative to the rear fork end (51) at a predetermined orientation; characterized in that: the first connection structure (8a) and the second connection structure (8b) are arranged such that, when the bracket body (8) is mounted on the rear fork end (51), a connection point provided by the first connection structure (8a) is, when viewed from the rear fork end (51), below and behind a connection point provided by the second connection structure (8b)." Shimano Co., Ltd. stated in the patent specification for that amendment: "The present invention provides a bracket which, when connected to a derailleur mounting extension, provides an appropriate connection position for a derailleur to be mounted on a bicycle frame, such that a derailleur connected to the bracket can easily assume an appropriate mounting posture." The State Intellectual Property Office, in its second Office Action, considered that the prior art had already disclosed a connection mechanism for connecting a derailleur to a bicycle frame, and that the technical solution defined in claim 1 lacked novelty with respect to the prior art disclosed in the cited document. In response to the second Office Action of the State Intellectual Property Office, Shimano Co., Ltd. made the following statement: "The applicant has further limited new claim 1 to more clearly describe the characteristics that distinguish the mounting method of the present invention from that of the prior art bicycle derailleur in the cited document; the derailleur in the cited document is directly mounted on the derailleur mounting extension of the rear fork end of the bicycle frame, whereas the present invention connects the bracket member (5) of the rear derailleur to one end of the bracket body (8) of the bracket, and then connects the other end of the bracket body (8) to the derailleur mounting extension (14) of the rear fork end (51) of the bicycle frame." Pursuant to the second Office Action of the State Intellectual Property Office, Shimano Co., Ltd. again amended claim 1 of the patent-in-suit to the form of claim 1 in the granted text.

Richen Company offered for sale the accused infringing products, bicycle rear derailleurs of models RD-HG-30A and RD-HG-40A, in its corporate product sample catalog. The First Notary Office of Huangpu District, Shanghai, at the request of Shanghai Huacheng Law Firm, notarized the process of evidence preservation in which personnel of Shanghai Huacheng Law Firm purchased the accused infringing products, RD-HG-30A and RD-HG-40A bicycle rear derailleurs, from Richen Company on January 15, 2003, and sealed the purchased accused infringing products. Since the accused infringing products had not yet been installed on a bicycle, they did not have the technical feature of claim 1 of the patent-in-suit, "the bicycle frame having a connection structure (14a) formed on a derailleur mounting extension (14) of a rear fork end (51) of the bicycle frame," nor could the specific installation method of the accused infringing products on a bicycle be determined. Shimano Co., Ltd. argued that the accused infringing products could only be installed, during use, on a bicycle frame as described in claim 1 of the patent-in-suit using the installation method provided by the patent-in-suit; otherwise, they could not be used. Richen Company, however, argued that the accused infringing products lacked the bicycle frame described in claim 1 of the patent-in-suit and the relevant essential technical features corresponding to the frame, and therefore did not constitute infringement. On September 9, 2004, the court of first instance, upon Shimano Co., Ltd.'s application, went to Richen Company's business premises to conduct evidence preservation. Upon inspection, no accused infringing products (RD-HG-30A and RD-HG-40A bicycle rear derailleurs) or special molds for manufacturing the accused infringing products were found. Shimano Co., Ltd. had retained attorneys to investigate, collect evidence, and litigate this case, but the attorney fees paid by Shimano Co., Ltd. for this case could not be determined due to insufficient evidence provided. Apart from that, Shimano Co., Ltd. had incurred reasonable expenses for this case totaling RMB 3,592.85.

The court of first instance held that Shimano Co., Ltd. was the patentee of the patent-in-suit, which was valid and protected by law. With respect to whether the physical accused infringing products, RD-HG-30A and RD-HG-40A bicycle rear derailleurs, were manufactured by Richen Company, since the accused infringing products were purchased by personnel of Shanghai Huacheng Law Firm from Richen Company's business premises, the purchase process was notarized by the First Notary Office of Huangpu District, Shanghai, and the accused infringing products bore Richen Company's "SUNRUN" trademark, the accused infringing products could be determined to have been manufactured by Richen Company. Because the accused infringing products provided by Shimano Co., Ltd. had not yet been installed on a bicycle, they naturally did not have the technical feature of claim 1, "the bicycle frame having a connection structure (14a) formed on a derailleur mounting extension (14) of a rear fork end (51) of the bicycle frame," nor was the specific installation method clear. Shimano Co., Ltd. argued that in actual use, the accused infringing products would inevitably possess all the essential technical features described in the patent-in-suit, while Richen Company denied this. Therefore, the focus of the case was whether the accused infringing products would inevitably possess all the essential technical features described in the patent-in-suit during use. Comparing claim 1 of the granted text of the patent-in-suit with claim 1 of the original published text, it was clear that Shimano Co., Ltd. had made significant narrowing amendments to the scope of protection in order to obtain the patent. Claim 1 of the first published original text did not limit the bicycle frame structure on which the rear derailleur bracket was installed or the specific installation method. Claim 1 of the second published original text, after amendment, limited the bicycle frame structure on which the rear derailleur bracket was installed, i.e., "the bicycle frame having a connection structure (14a) formed on a derailleur mounting extension (14) of a rear fork end (51) of the bicycle frame." That is, the rear derailleur bracket could only constitute infringement if it was installed on a bicycle frame having the structure described in the patent. This specific bicycle frame structure constituted one of the essential technical features of the patent. The final granted text, in addition to making the same limitation on the bicycle frame structure, also limited the specific installation method. Only under this premise did Shimano Co., Ltd. obtain the grant of the patent-in-suit. Therefore, the specific bicycle frame structure and the specific installation method described in claim 1 of the patent-in-suit were two essential technical features of the patent. According to Shimano Co., Ltd.'s assertion that the accused infringing products would inevitably possess all the essential technical features described in the patent-in-suit during actual use, then Shimano Co., Ltd. would have clearly written all essential technical features when it first drafted the patent claims; otherwise, the patent would be inoperable, but the facts were otherwise. Before Shimano Co., Ltd. had limited the specific bicycle frame structure and the specific installation method, the State Intellectual Property Office considered that the "rear derailleur bracket" constituted prior art and lacked novelty, thus precluding the grant of a patent. On the one hand, this indicated that the "rear derailleur bracket" could be installed on other types of bicycle frames, otherwise it would not constitute prior art. On the other hand, it also indicated that Shimano Co., Ltd. originally wished for the "rear derailleur bracket" to be installable on a wider range of bicycle frames, but only because it could not obtain a patent did it limit the structure of the bicycle frame on which the "rear derailleur bracket" was installed and the installation method. It follows that Shimano Co., Ltd.'s view that the accused infringing products could only be installed on a bicycle frame having the structure described in claim 1 using the installation method provided by the patent-in-suit during use, and otherwise could not be used, was inconsistent with the facts and with Shimano Co., Ltd.'s actions during the patent application process. That view was not adopted. A patent claim is a complete technical solution composed of technical features of the invention. The scope of protection of an invention patent is determined by the content of the claims. When determining the scope of patent protection, a court must strictly follow the claims, must not arbitrarily reduce the technical features of the claims to expand the scope of patent protection, and must not allow a patentee to restrict and narrow the scope of protection in order to obtain the patent, and then make a contrary interpretation after obtaining the patent. Since the rear derailleur bracket of the patent-in-suit could be installed on other types of bicycle frames, and the accused infringing products had not yet been installed on a bicycle, it was unclear whether after installation they would possess the essential technical feature "the bicycle frame having a connection structure (14a) formed on a derailleur mounting extension (14) of a rear fork end (51) of the bicycle frame" and whether the installation method was as described in the claim of the patent-in-suit. Therefore, the conditions for comparison to determine whether the accused infringing products constituted infringement were not yet satisfied. Shimano Co., Ltd.'s claim that the accused infringing products had already constituted infringement was not established and was not supported. Pursuant to Article 64, Paragraph 1 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 56, Paragraph 1 of the Patent Law of the People's Republic of China, the Ningbo Intermediate People's Court of Zhejiang Province rendered the Civil Judgment (2004) Yong Min Er Chu Zi No. 240 on March 15, 2005, dismissing all of Shimano Co., Ltd.'s claims. The case acceptance fee was RMB 7,010, and the evidence preservation fee was RMB 1,000, totaling RMB 8,010, to be borne by Shimano Co., Ltd.

Shimano Inc., dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Zhejiang High People's Court of the People's Republic of China. The court of second instance focused its review on the following evidence.

1. During the first instance, Shimano Inc. submitted the "Industry Standard of the People's Republic of China - Bicycle Industry Standard - Bicycle Frame" (QB1880-93), seeking to prove that bicycle frames manufactured in accordance with the industry standard must possess the extension part described in the patent-in-suit, that the accused infringing product must be installed on a bicycle by means of said installation extension part, and thus that such technical feature necessarily falls within the scope of protection of the patent-in-suit. After cross-examination at the first-instance trial, Richun Company argued that this industry standard is not part of the specification of the patent-in-suit, cannot be used to interpret the scope of the patent claims, and has no relevance to this case. The industry standard provides technical specifications for frames, including both frames with extension parts and frames without extension parts; that is, the industry standard does not require all bicycle frames to have an extension part. The standard cannot lead to the conclusion that installing the accused infringing product on a bicycle necessarily falls within the scope of patent protection, nor can it be used to interpret the scope of protection of the patent-in-suit. Accordingly, the first-instance court found that this evidence was not relevant to the case, and this finding was not improper.

2. During the first-instance trial, Richun Company argued that its product could be installed on bicycle frames without an extension part and conducted an on-site demonstration. Shimano Inc. argued that Richun Company's direct installation of its product on a bicycle frame without an extension part involved adding a washer, which constituted the addition of a technical feature and could not be deemed as not falling within the scope of patent protection, and then demonstrated the installation effect after removing the washer. The first-instance court did not rule on this factual matter in its judgment, which was improper. The court of second instance held that, based on the demonstration during the first-instance trial, the accused infringing product could be directly installed on a bicycle without a bracket extension part by adding a washer. Installation by adding a washer is a publicly known, conventional mechanical installation technique, and it cannot be considered that the accused infringing product cannot be used normally if installed on a bicycle without a bracket extension part. Therefore, the first-instance judgment's finding that the accused infringing product could be installed on other structures of bicycle frames was not improper.

3. During the second-instance trial, Shimano Inc. submitted two notarized evidence preservation documents: first, a notarial certificate issued on May 9, 2005 by the First Notary Public Office of Huangpu District, Shanghai. It stated that on May 6, 2005, personnel from Shanghai Huacheng Law Firm, together with notarial staff, went to the 15th China International Bicycle Exhibition held at the Shanghai New International Expo Centre and obtained an instance of the installation state of the accused infringing product manufactured by Richun Company used on a bicycle of Hangzhou Junqi Bicycle Industry Co., Ltd. This was intended to prove that the accused infringing product could only be installed on a specific bicycle frame. Second, a notarial certificate issued on June 13, 2005 by the Gongshu District Notary Public Office, Hangzhou. It stated that on May 23, 2005, personnel from Zhejiang Tiance Law Firm, together with notarial staff, went to the Zhejiang Bicycle Market and obtained an instance of the state of a mountain bicycle sold by Hangzhou Jiangkai Hardware, Electrical, and Chemical Co., Ltd. and manufactured by Shenzhen Xidesheng Bicycle Co., Ltd., which allegedly infringed the patent-in-suit. This was intended to prove that the accused infringing product manufactured by Richun Company could only be installed on that specific bicycle frame in the specific manner shown in the instance. After cross-examination at trial, Richun Company argued: regarding the first notarial certificate, Hangzhou Junqi Bicycle Industry Co., Ltd. had no connection with Richun Company, and the bicycle displayed was also unrelated to Richun Company; the photographs taken during notarization could not show the structure of the rear derailleur and could not be compared with the patented technology; the bicycle frame in the notarized evidence was not manufactured by Richun Company, and Richun Company had not engaged in the act of installing the rear derailleur on that frame. Regarding the second notarial certificate, it could not show any connection between Shenzhen Xidesheng Bicycle Co., Ltd. and Richun Company; the photographs taken could not show the structure of the rear derailleur and the frame; the frame was not manufactured by Richun Company, and the act of installing the rear derailleur was not performed by Richun Company. The court of second instance held that the authenticity of the above notarial documents was recognized in the absence of sufficient evidence from Richun Company to overturn them; however, the contents of the two notarial certificates could not prove that there was a legal connection between the two bicycle manufacturers and Richun Company, nor could they prove that the act of installing the rear derailleur onto the frame was completed by Richun Company. From the perspective of the installation method, they could at most prove that two bicycle manufacturers had connected and installed the accused infringing product onto the extension part of the rear frame of the bicycle in a certain identical manner, but could not prove that all accused infringing products necessarily required that method to be connected to the rear frame of a bicycle. Therefore, these two pieces of evidence could not yet prove that Richun Company had engaged in infringement of the patent-in-suit.

4. During the appeal, Shimano Inc. submitted an application for evidence collection, requesting that the court of second instance investigate the assembly condition of the complete bicycle at Hangzhou Junqi Bicycle Industry Co., Ltd. to ascertain the actual usage state of the accused infringing product. The court of second instance, upon review, held that Shimano Inc. had already provided evidence in this regard through notarized evidence collection during the second-instance trial, and that the application did not meet the requirements of Articles 15 and 17 of the Supreme People's Court's "Several Provisions on Evidence in Civil Proceedings," and therefore denied the application.

The court of second instance held that, according to the claims of the patent-in-suit, the main technical features of the patent-in-suit included two parts: structural features and installation features. Shimano Inc. agreed with this. Comparing the accused infringing product with the structural features of the patent-in-suit, both were identical, and the parties had no dispute on this point. The focus of the dispute in this case was whether the accused infringing product possessed the installation features of the patent-in-suit. The first-instance court, considering the patentee's written statement made during patent examination to ensure the novelty of the patent, which limited the scope of protection of the patent claims, defined the installation features of the patent-in-suit, and this was not improper. According to independent claim 1 and the patentee's written statement during patent examination, the installation features of the patent-in-suit were: the bicycle frame having a connecting structure (14a) formed on a derailleur installation extension part (14) of a rear fork end (51) of the bicycle frame; and the arrangement of the first connecting structure (8a) and the second connecting structure (8b) such that when the bracket body (8) is installed on the rear fork end (51), the connection point provided by the first connecting structure (8a) is below and behind the connection point provided by the second connecting structure (8b). That is, at least the following two installation features were present: (1) a bicycle frame having a rear fork end; (2) installation on the extension part of the rear fork end of the frame. The accused infringing product manufactured by Richun Company only possessed the structural features of the patent claim; Richun Company did not perform any installation act; the accused infringing product did not possess the installation features of the patent claim, did not fall within the scope of protection of the patent-in-suit, and did not constitute patent infringement. During the second-instance trial, Shimano Inc. further argued that although Richun Company did not itself perform the installation, others who used the accused infringing product would necessarily install it in the manner described by the installation features of the patent-in-suit, which at least constituted indirect infringement. In response, the court of second instance held that there are no provisions on indirect patent infringement in Chinese patent laws and regulations; in judicial practice, a finding of indirect patent infringement requires the existence of direct patent infringement as a prerequisite. Since there was no direct infringement in this case, Richun Company could not be found to have committed indirect infringement. Based on the above, the patent-in-suit included both structural features and installation features, but the accused infringing product only possessed the structural features of the patent-in-suit; Richun Company did not perform any installation act, and the accused infringing product could also be installed by means other than those defined in the patent-in-suit. Therefore, Richun Company's conduct did not constitute patent infringement. The first-instance judgment found clear facts and correctly applied the law. Pursuant to Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Zhejiang High People's Court rendered a civil judgment on October 28, 2005, (2005) Zhe Min San Zhong Zi No. 145, as follows: the appeal was dismissed and the original judgment was affirmed. The second-instance case acceptance fee of RMB 7,010 was borne by Shimano Inc.

Shimano Inc., dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment, applied to this Court for retrial. This Court issued a civil ruling on October 20, 2009, (2008) Min Jian Zi No. 197, instructing the Zhejiang High People's Court to conduct a retrial. During the retrial stage, neither party provided new evidence.

The Zhejiang High People's Court held in the retrial that the focus of the dispute in this case was whether the accused infringing product fell within the scope of protection of the patent-in-suit. First, regarding the issue raised by Shimano Inc. whether the original trial court's division of the technical features of claim 1 of the patent-in-suit and its finding that the accused infringing product did not fall within the scope of patent protection were appropriate. Claim 1 of the patent-in-suit is: 1) Preamble: A bicycle rear derailleur bracket for connecting a rear derailleur (100) to a bicycle frame (50), the rear derailleur having a bracket member (5), a support member (4) for supporting a chain guide (3), and a pair of connecting members (6, 7) for connecting the support member (4) and the bracket member (5), the bicycle frame having a connecting structure (14a) formed on a derailleur installation extension part (14) of a rear fork end (51) of the bicycle frame, the rear derailleur bracket comprising: a bracket body (8) formed of a generally L-shaped plate; a first connecting structure (8a) provided near one end of the bracket body (8) for connecting the bracket member (5) of the rear derailleur (100) to the bracket body (8) and pivotable about a first axis (91); a second connecting structure (8b) provided near the other end of the bracket body (8) for connecting the bracket body (8) to the connecting structure (14a) of the bicycle frame (50); and a positioning structure (8c) for contacting the derailleur installation extension part (14) to position the rear derailleur (100) in a predetermined posture relative to the rear fork end (51). 2) Characterizing portion: Characterized in that the arrangement of the first connecting structure (8a) and the second connecting structure (8b) is such that when the bracket body (8) is installed on the rear fork end (51), the connection point provided by the first connecting structure (8a) is below and behind the connection point provided by the second connecting structure (8b). According to the above expression of the claim, its main technical features should include structural features and installation features, wherein the expressions embodying the installation features are: "the bicycle frame having a connecting structure (14a) formed on a derailleur installation extension part (14) of a rear fork end (51) of the bicycle frame; the arrangement of the first connecting structure (8a) and the second connecting structure (8b) such that when the bracket body (8) is installed on the rear fork end (51), the connection point provided by the first connecting structure (8a) is below and behind the connection point provided by the second connecting structure (8b)." That is, the patent-in-suit at least possesses two installation features: (1) a bicycle frame having a rear fork end; (2) the bracket body being installed on the rear fork end of the bicycle. Shimano Inc. denied this division of the technical features of the patent-in-suit during the retrial stage, which was inconsistent with both the expression of the patent claim and its own agreement with this division during the second instance and its clear statement when applying for the patent ("the installation method of the bicycle derailleur of the present invention is a different feature from Comparative Document 3"). Although the structural features of the accused infringing product were identical to those of the patented product, because the claim of the patent-in-suit included specific installation features, and the accused infringing product had not yet been installed on a bicycle, it was not clear whether, after installation, it would necessarily possess all the installation features described in the claim. The applicant for retrial argued that in actual use, the accused infringing product would necessarily possess all the essential technical features described in the patent-in-suit. However, on the one hand, before Shimano Inc. made specific limitations on the bicycle frame structure and installation method, the State Intellectual Property Office considered the rear derailleur bracket to be prior art, lacking novelty, indicating that this "rear derailleur bracket" could be installed not only on bicycle frames having a rear fork end but also on other structures of bicycle frames. On the other hand, Richun Company demonstrated in the first-instance court that by adding a washer, the accused infringing product could be directly installed on a bicycle without a bracket extension part, showing that conventional mechanical installation techniques could avoid the accused infringing product falling within the scope of patent protection. Therefore, the inference by Shimano Inc. was not sufficiently substantiated. Shimano Inc. had not yet been able to prove that Richun Company's conduct constituted infringement of the patent-in-suit. Second, regarding the issue raised by Shimano Inc. that the original trial court either did not admit or did not cross-examine two important pieces of evidence. As for the "Industry Standard of the People's Republic of China - Bicycle Industry Standard - Bicycle Frame" (QB1880-93) submitted by Shimano Inc., this industry standard does not require all bicycle frames to have an extension part, cannot be used to interpret the scope of protection of the patent-in-suit, and even less can it prove that the accused infringing product falls within the scope of patent protection. The original trial court's decision not to admit this evidence was not improper. During the first instance, the parties each conducted an on-site demonstration of the installation effect of the accused infringing product on a bicycle. The first-instance judgment did not describe this situation, but the second-instance judgment made a corresponding correction. Therefore, the relevant grounds for retrial by Shimano Inc. were also untenable. In summary, the main technical features of the patent-in-suit included structural features and installation features. Although the accused infringing product possessed the structural features of the patent, because Richun Company did not perform an installation act, and Shimano Inc. could not prove that the accused infringing product would necessarily possess the installation features described in the patent claim, Richun Company's accused conduct did not constitute infringement. The grounds for retrial by Shimano Inc. were untenable and were not supported. The original trial judgment's findings of fact and application of law were not improper and should be affirmed. Pursuant to Article 186, Paragraph 1 and Article 153, Paragraph 1, Item (1) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, the Zhejiang High People's Court rendered a civil judgment on August 26, 2010, (2009) Zhe Min Zai Zi No. 135, affirming the court's (2005) Zhe Min San Zhong Zi No. 145 civil judgment.

Shimano Inc., dissatisfied with the retrial judgment, applied to this Court for a retrial. The main grounds are as follows: (I) The retrial judgment erred in the determination of the patent protection scope and the application of law in the infringement determination. 1. The basis for determining the scope of patent protection is the essential technical features explicitly recorded in the claims, not all the language in the claims. Explanatory, use-related, and descriptive words and statements appearing in the claims may help understand the claims but do not affect the scope of patent protection. The subject matter of the patent in this case is a bracket for a rear derailleur, not a bicycle or a rear derailleur. The technical features concerning the bicycle rear derailleur bracket are the essential technical features of the patent in this case, while technical features related to other products obviously do not constitute essential technical features of the patent in this case. The technical features “the rear derailleur has a bracket member (5), a support member (4) for supporting a chain guide (3), and a pair of connecting members (6, 7) for connecting the support member (4) and the bracket member (5)” and “the bicycle frame has a connecting structure (14a) formed on a derailleur mounting extension (14) of a rear fork end (51) of the bicycle frame” serve to provide a defining description of the rear derailleur and the bicycle frame, thereby clarifying their specific application fields and usage scope, and are unrelated to the technical subject matter of the patent in this case. The above two technical features do not limit the components or characteristics of the rear derailleur bracket; they merely limit its use. As long as the accused infringing product covers all essential technical features and can be used to connect the rear derailleur to the bicycle frame, it falls within the protection scope of the patent in this case, without requiring that the accused infringing product be actually installed on a specific bicycle. 2. Claim 1 of the patent in this case is a product claim. For a product claim containing use and functional features, the subject of protection remains the product, not the act of using or installing that product. The retrial judgment erroneously divided the technical features of claim 1 into structural features and installation features, and further found that claim 1 at least had two installation features: a bicycle frame with a rear fork end; and the bracket body being installed on the rear fork end of the bicycle. The so-called installation feature refers to the installation act of the actor. This division and finding are clearly without legal basis, lack logic, and violate the basic meaning of technical features. 3. The technical feature in claim 1 of the patent in this case, “the first connecting structure (8a) and the second connecting structure (8b) are arranged such that when the bracket body (8) is installed on the rear fork end (51), the connection point provided by the first connecting structure (8a) is below and behind the connection point provided by the second connecting structure (8b),” is a functional description of the rear derailleur bracket. As long as a rear derailleur bracket having the structural features defined in claim 1 of the patent in this case can be installed on the bicycle frame defined in claim 1 of this case, the positional relationship between its first connecting structure and second connecting structure will appear as described in that technical feature. 4. The structural diagram of the accused infringing product RD-HG-40A is almost identical to Figures 1 and 5 of the patent specification in this case, constituting literal infringement of the patent in this case. The retrial judgment’s division of the technical features of the patent in this case into structural features and installation features leads to an erroneous understanding of the scope of protection of the claims. The retrial judgment’s use of whether the actor performed the installation act as the basis for determining infringement clearly violates the provisions of the Patent Law. In fact, installing the bicycle accessory defined in claim 1 of the patent in this case onto a bicycle is the actor’s act of using the patented product. (II) The retrial judgment’s factual finding that the accused infringing product could be installed not only on a bicycle frame with a rear fork end but also on bicycle frames with other structures lacks a basis. 1. The assertion that the accused infringing product could also be installed on bicycle frames of other structures was a unilateral statement by Richen Co., Ltd., unsupported by any pre-existing actual installed products, or any relevant literature or third-party testimony. 2. During the first-instance trial, Richen Co., Ltd. demonstrated installing the accused infringing product directly on a bicycle without a rear fork end derailleur mounting extension by adding a washer. However, such installation is not an industrial/commercial installation; it is merely temporarily installing the accused infringing product on such a bicycle. The accused infringing product was sold without a washer, but instead included bolt M10 and positioning structure 8c. Richen Co., Ltd.’s use of the washer was precisely to compensate for the gap created by the positioning structure 8c on the accused infringing product. The installation method with a washer cannot accurately position the rear derailleur on the frame and does not meet the requirements of industrial production. (III) The retrial judgment’s determination that the patent prosecution history limited the scope of patent protection lacks factual basis. 1. During the examination of the patent in this case, a first amendment added reference numerals and adjusted the description; a second amendment added an explanation of the “rear derailleur” related to the use of the technical subject matter. Such use limitation did not affect the structure of the product itself. The rear derailleur bracket of the patent in this case was found to have novelty and inventiveness upon overall examination, and no limiting amendment or commitment was made regarding the scope of protection of the claims. 2. The difference between the patent in this case and the prior art lies in connecting (installing) the rear derailleur to a bicycle frame having a rear fork end derailleur mounting extension via a bracket body 8. It should be noted that both the rear derailleur and the bicycle frame having the rear fork end derailleur mounting extension existed before the filing date of the patent in this case, while the rear derailleur bracket described in claim 1 is a patentable technical solution of the present invention for improving the shifting performance of the rear derailleur. The Patent Office of the PRC never concluded that “the rear derailleur bracket was prior art” during the examination of the patent application in this case. (IV) The retrial judgment’s determination of evidence is erroneous. 1. The patent in this case relates to a component of bicycle industrial production, which must comply with certain industry standards; otherwise, it cannot be installed and matched. The “Industry Standard of the People’s Republic of China - Bicycle Industry Standard - Bicycle Frame” (QB1880-93) can prove that a bicycle frame can have an extension, and the accused infringing product can be installed on such a bicycle. At the same time, this standard can prove that Richen Co., Ltd.’s installation method using a washer had no basis in industry standards. The retrial judgment erred in not admitting this evidence. 2. During the first-instance and second-instance trials in this case, Shimano Inc. demonstrated on-site the assembly of the accused infringing product onto a bicycle. This evidence precisely proves that the accused infringing product can fulfill the use of the rear derailleur bracket as defined in claim 1 of the patent in this case, can be installed on the bicycle frame defined in the claims of the patent in this case, and possesses all the technical features of claim 1. The retrial court erred in not admitting this evidence. In summary, Shimano Inc., pursuant to Article 179, paragraph 1, items (2), (6), and (12) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People’s Republic of China, requests that the retrial judgment (2009) Zhe Min Zai Zi No. 135, the second-instance civil judgment (2005) Zhe Min San Zhong Zi No. 145, and the first-instance civil judgment (2004) Yong Min Er Chu Zi No. 240 be reversed; and that its entire claim be upheld, with litigation costs borne by Richen Co., Ltd.

Richen Co., Ltd. submitted opinions stating: (I) The scope of patent protection is defined by all technical features recorded in the claims. All technical features written into an independent claim are essential technical features and should not be ignored. The use or functional features or use-condition features recorded in claim 1 of the patent in this case, because they are explicitly written into the independent claim, are all essential technical features and should be considered in the comparison. The object of protection of the patent in this case is not the rear derailleur bracket itself, nor the rear derailleur assembled with the bracket body, but rather the assembly solution in which the rear derailleur is installed on the frame extension via the bracket body. (II) The accused infringing product lacks several essential technical features of the patent in this case and does not fall within its scope of protection. The accused infringing product does not have a frame; it does not form an installation connection relationship between the bracket body and the frame; it does not reflect the predetermined posture that “the connection point provided by the first connecting structure (8a) is below and behind the connection point provided by the second connecting structure (8b)” that necessarily results when the rear derailleur is installed on the frame; therefore, it does not constitute infringement. (III) The multiple essential technical features that the accused infringing product lacks are precisely the technical features amended by Shimano Inc. during the patent grant process. These emphasized and added technical features have a substantial impact on the scope of patent protection, limiting the scope of protection of claim 1. According to the prosecution history of the patent in this case, Shimano Inc. made the following amendments during the substantive examination: 1. Amending the attribute phrase before the name “rear derailleur bracket” in claim 1 of the published patent application to clearly limit the frame structure, thereby emphasizing that the “derailleur mounting extension of the rear fork end” corresponds to the “vertical drop component” of frame 12 in cited document 1, and that the “bracket body 8” of the patent in this case differs from the “suspension member 18” in cited document 1. 2. Moving the “bracket body 8” into the preamble as a feature common with the prior art, and designating the predetermined posture positional relationship of “behind and below” manifested when the “bracket body 8” is assembled onto the frame as the only characterizing feature. The reason for the amendment was to further limit claim 1 and more clearly describe that the installation method of the bicycle derailleur of the present invention is different from that of the cited document. This indicates that the patentee emphasized and confirmed that the “different installation method” is the only distinguishing feature of the patent in this case. 3. Amending the derailleur described in claim 1 of the published patent application to be “composed of a bracket member 5, a chain guide 3, a support member 4, and connecting members 6 and 7,” thereby distinguishing the “bracket body 8” from the “base member 1” in cited document 3. This amendment indicates that the rear derailleur and its bracket body are prior art and are not patentable per se; only the assembly of the rear derailleur using the bracket body with a specific bicycle frame meets the grant conditions. (IV) Shimano Inc. filed another divisional patent application for a rear derailleur based on the patent in this case. During the amendment process, the divisional patent deleted technical features such as the bicycle frame, and the Patent Reexamination Board of the State Intellectual Property Office (hereinafter referred to as the Patent Reexamination Board) declared the entire divisional patent invalid due to the amendment exceeding the scope. Therefore, the bicycle frame and installation structure features should not be ignored in this case. (V) The accused infringing product in this case is a universal bracket body, not exclusively usable on frame rear fork ends with a derailleur mounting extension. (VI) There are multiple grounds on which the patent in this case could be declared invalid. The proceedings in this case should be stayed. Richen Co., Ltd. has already filed a request for invalidation of the patent in this case with the Patent Reexamination Board, which has been accepted.

This Court finds upon examination that the facts found in the first-instance, second-instance, and retrial judgments are true.

This Court further finds: During the first-instance, second-instance, and retrial proceedings, Shimano Inc. has always relied on claim 1 of the patent in this case as the basis for its claims.

To prove that the accused infringing product can only be installed on the rear fork end of a bicycle frame having a derailleur mounting extension connecting structure as defined in the patent in this case, Shimano Inc. submitted the following evidence during the first-instance and second-instance proceedings: physical samples of the accused infringing products RD-HG-30A and RD-HG-40A bicycle rear derailleurs and their brackets (First Instance Evidence No. 6); the “Industry Standard of the People’s Republic of China - Bicycle Industry Standard - Bicycle Frame” (QB1880-93) (First Instance Evidence No. 18); Shimano Inc. demonstrated on-site the assembly of the accused infringing product onto the rear fork end of a bicycle frame having a derailleur mounting extension connecting structure; notarized documents (2005) Hu Huang Yi Zheng Jing Zi No. 5137 and (2005) Hang Gong Zheng Jing Zi No. 475 (Second Instance Supplementary Evidence).

The accused infringing product in this case is a substantially L-shaped plate with a circular bolt hole at each end. One end is connected to the bicycle rear derailleur. Near the bolt hole away from the rear derailleur, there is a protruding portion that extends upward from the surface of the plate. Thus, the accused infringing product possesses the structural features of the bracket body in claim 1 of the patent, namely: a bracket body formed by a substantially L-shaped plate; a first connecting structure provided near one end of the bracket body, for connecting the bracket member of the rear derailleur to the bracket body, pivotable about a first axis; a second connecting structure provided near the other end of the bracket body, for connecting the bracket body to the connecting structure of the bicycle frame; and a positioning structure for contacting the derailleur mounting extension so as to position the rear derailleur in a predetermined posture relative to the rear fork end. Meanwhile, the rear derailleur connected to the accused infringing product has the features described in claim 1 of the patent in this case, i.e., the rear derailleur has a bracket member, a support member for supporting a chain guide, and a pair of connecting members for connecting the support member and the bracket member. The “Industry Standard of the People’s Republic of China - Bicycle Industry Standard - Bicycle Frame” (QB1880-93) is a mandatory industry standard issued by the former Ministry of Light Industry of China. Figure 10 on page 7 of this standard shows two types of bicycle frame horizontal dropouts, one with a rear fork end extension and the other without. According to the notarized document (2005) Hu Huang Yi Zheng Jing Zi No. 5137, on May 6, 2005, personnel from Shanghai Huacheng Law Firm, together with a notary, went to the venue of the 15th China International Bicycle Fair held at the Shanghai New International Expo Center. The personnel from Shanghai Huacheng Law Firm obtained a product brochure from the booth of Hangzhou Junqi Bicycle Co., Ltd. and took 17 photographs at the exhibition. The photographs attached to the notarized document show that the rear fork end of the bicycle produced by Hangzhou Junqi Bicycle Co., Ltd. has a derailleur mounting extension, and the accused infringing product together with the rear derailleur is installed on the rear fork end of that bicycle, and the rear derailleur connected to the accused infringing product bears the trademark “SUNRUN” of Richen Co., Ltd. According to the notarized document (2005) Hang Gong Zheng Jing Zi No. 475, on May 23, 2005, Yang Lei, an agent of Zhejiang Tiance Law Firm, together with a notary, went to the stall of Hangzhou Jiangkai Hardware, Electrical Appliances, and Chemical Co., Ltd. in Zhejiang Bicycle Market. Yang Lei, as an ordinary consumer, purchased a mountain bicycle produced by Shenzhen Xidesheng Bicycle Co., Ltd. and took photographs of the bicycle. The photographs attached to the notarized document show that the rear fork end of the mountain bicycle has a derailleur mounting extension, and the accused infringing product together with the rear derailleur is installed on the rear fork end of that mountain bicycle, and the rear derailleur connected to the accused infringing product bears the trademark “SUNRUN” of Richen Co., Ltd.

To prove that the accused infringing product in this case could be installed on the rear fork end of a bicycle frame without a rear derailleur mounting extension, Richen Co., Ltd. performed an actual installation demonstration during the trial of the original instance. During the demonstration, Richen Co., Ltd. added a washer between the accused infringing product and the frame rear fork end to compensate for the gap caused by the protruding portion of the accused infringing product, thereby directly installing the accused infringing product onto the rear fork end of a bicycle without a rear derailleur mounting extension. Shimano Inc. argued that the need for a washer to compensate for the gap caused by the protruding portion precisely indicates that the corresponding portion of the protrusion is the rear fork end defined in the patent; adding a washer is not a normal industrial production method, is not secure, and then demonstrated the installation effect after removing the washer. During the retrial review and proceedings of this case, this Court requested Richen Co., Ltd. to submit evidence regarding bicycles on which the accused infringing product was installed on a frame without a rear fork end extension and that were already commercially circulated in the market. Richen Co., Ltd. was unable to provide such evidence.

Regarding the amendment process of the patent document in this case, this court additionally finds the following facts: The original published text of Shimano Inc.'s patent application contained the following claims: "1. A rear derailleur bracket for connecting a rear derailleur to a bicycle frame, formed on an extension of a rear fork end of the bicycle frame for mounting a gearshift, comprising: a bracket body; a first connecting structure provided near one end of the bracket body for connecting the rear derailleur to the bracket body; a second connecting structure provided near the other end of the bracket body for connecting the bracket body to the connecting structure of the bicycle frame; and a positioning structure for contacting the gearshift mounting extension to position the rear derailleur in a predetermined posture relative to the rear fork end. 2. The rear derailleur bracket of claim 1, wherein the bracket body is a substantially L-shaped plate, the first connecting structure and the second connecting structure are substantially circular bolt holes, and the positioning structure is located adjacent to the second connecting structure. 3. The rear derailleur bracket of claim 2, wherein the positioning structure is a protrusion extending substantially perpendicularly from the surface of the plate. 4. The rear derailleur bracket of claim 1, wherein the arrangement of the first connecting structure and the second connecting structure is such that when the bracket body is installed on the rear fork end, the connection point provided by the second connecting structure is below and behind the connection point provided by the first connecting structure as viewed from the rear fork end." On May 22, 1997, the former Patent Office of the People's Republic of China issued a first office action to Shimano Inc. This office action cited U.S. Patent No. 5,082,303 (Document 1) and European Patent EP 0,013,136 (Document 2), both prior to the priority date of the patent in question, and considered that claim 1 of the patent lacked novelty, claims 2 and 3 lacked inventiveness, and claim 4 did not comply with Article 26, paragraph 4 of the Patent Law, and therefore the patent application would be rejected. The text of the office action stated: "2. Claim 4 further limits the technical solution of claim 1. However, this claim cannot be accepted because it does not comply with Article 26, paragraph 4 of the Patent Law. Specifically, the claim is not supported by the description. Specifically, from the description of the embodiment (e.g., Figure 1), it can be clearly understood that the connection point provided by the second connecting structure, as viewed from the rear fork end, is obviously above and behind, rather than below and behind, the connection point provided by the first connecting structure. Therefore, the claim cannot be accepted due to lack of support from the description. It should be noted that even if the applicant modifies it to 'above and behind' based on the description to comply with Article 26, paragraph 4 of the Patent Law, such a technical solution would still not be accepted because it does not comply with the requirement of inventiveness under Article 22, paragraph 3 of the Patent Law. This is because designing the relative positions of the two connection points according to actual needs is easy for a person of ordinary skill in the art. Moreover, the two connection points of the rear derailleur mounting bracket disclosed in Document 2 meet the above relative positional relationship — see Figure 10 of Document 1. At the same time, this structure does not produce any new unexpected effects."

In response to the above office action, Shimano Inc. amended the claims and submitted a statement of opinions. This amendment primarily merged original claims 1 and 4 into a new claim 1, made textual adjustments to the preamble to clarify the subject matter of claim 1, and made minor textual changes to original claims 2 and 3. After this amendment, the claims read as follows: "1. A rear derailleur bracket for connecting a rear derailleur (100) to a bicycle frame (50), the bicycle frame having a connecting structure (14a) formed on a gearshift mounting extension (14) of a rear fork end (51) of the bicycle frame, the rear derailleur bracket comprising: a bracket body (8); a first connecting structure (8a) provided near one end of the bracket body (8) for connecting the rear derailleur (100) to the bracket body (8); a second connecting structure (8b) provided near the other end of the bracket body (8) for connecting the bracket body (8) to the connecting structure (14a) of the bicycle frame (50); and a positioning structure (8c) for contacting the gearshift mounting extension (14) to position the rear derailleur (100) in a predetermined posture relative to the rear fork end (51); characterized in that: the arrangement of the first connecting structure (8a) and the second connecting structure (8b) is such that when the bracket body (8) is installed on the rear fork end (51), the connection point provided by the first connecting structure (8a) is below and behind the connection point provided by the second connecting structure (8b) as viewed from the rear fork end (51). 2. The rear derailleur bracket of claim 1, characterized in that the bracket body (8) is formed of a substantially L-shaped plate, the first connecting structure (8a) and the second connecting structure (8b) are in the form of substantially circular bolt holes, and the positioning structure (8c) is located adjacent to the second connecting structure (8b). 3. The rear derailleur bracket of claim 2, characterized in that the positioning structure (8c) is a protrusion extending from the surface of the plate." In the same statement of opinions, Shimano Inc. further stated: "(I) The applicant now describes the prior art with reference to Document 1. The hanger member (18) described in Document 1 is a replaceable part of a vertical drop assembly. For the following reasons, Document 1 does not suggest or disclose the bracket body (8) as claimed in the present application: 1) The title of Document 1 is 'Replaceable Drop Assembly,' thus it only relates to a vertical drop assembly and does not relate to the bracket member (8) of the present application. 2) Claim 1 of Document 1 recites 'a vertical drop assembly comprising: a vertical drop member (16); a hanger member (18); a means for connecting the hanger member to the drop member;...' This indicates that the hanger member (18) in Document 1 is part of the vertical drop assembly. ... 4) The design of the vertical drop assembly shown in Figure 2 of Document 1 is the same as that of the rear fork end (51) with rear derailleur mounting extension (14) described in the present application; Figure 5 of the present application most clearly shows the structure of the rear fork end (51) with rear derailleur mounting extension (14). 5) The rear derailleur shown in Figure 1 of Document 1 is a direct-mount type, wherein the derailleur (50) is directly mounted to the vertical drop assembly without using a bracket body (8) as in the present application. 6) Document 1 does not mention or disclose a bracket body (8) as in the present application for connecting the rear derailleur (50) to the hanger member (18). 7) In the past, vertical drop assemblies have always been used with direct-mount type rear derailleurs, and until now, there has been no connection of a rear derailleur with a bracket body to a vertical drop assembly. The bracket body of the present application makes it possible to connect a rear derailleur to a vertical drop assembly. 8) The vertical drop member (16) shown in Figure 3 of Document 1 does not disclose or suggest connecting a direct-mount type rear derailleur thereto. On the contrary, it shows the derailleur mounted to the hanger member (18). This further indicates that the vertical drop member (16) is not configured to mount the derailleur, and the hanger member (18) needs to be considered as part of the drop member (16) that is sometimes disassembled, rather than as a bracket. ... (II) Regarding Document 2 (EP 0,013,136), the fork end described in Document 2 is a drop assembly with a horizontal slot. Document 2 does not disclose or suggest the features of the present application. In particular, a bracket body is not connected to a vertical drop (assembly) or an L-shaped plate. (III) Regarding the present invention, the preamble of newly amended claim 1 recites: 'A rear derailleur bracket for connecting a rear derailleur (100) to a bicycle frame (50), the bicycle frame having a connecting structure (14a) formed on a gearshift mounting extension (14) of a rear fork end (51) of the bicycle frame.' It can be seen that the bracket body (8) disclosed in the present invention is connected to a vertical drop (assembly). Therefore, the subject matter and features of the bracket body (8) of the present invention are clear and possess novelty and inventiveness. ... Claim 2 of the present application limits the feature that 'the bracket body (8) is formed of a substantially L-shaped plate.' This is an important feature that enables the bracket body (8) to be connected to the drop assembly (hanger member 18) while maintaining the rear derailleur in an appropriate posture as described in the specification. The applicant believes that this additional feature also possesses novelty and inventiveness...."

In response to the above statement of opinions, the State Intellectual Property Office issued a second office action, citing U.S. Patent No. 4,690,663 as Document 3, considering that the amended claim 1 of the patent application lacked novelty and claim 2 lacked inventiveness. The text of the office action stated: "1. Independent claim 1 claims protection for a rear derailleur bracket for connecting a rear derailleur to a bicycle frame. Document 3 discloses a connecting mechanism for connecting a rear derailleur to a bicycle frame, specifically disclosing the following technical content: one end of a base member 1 (corresponding to bracket member 8 of the present application) is connected to a threaded hole 101b (corresponding to connecting structure 14a of the present application) on the gearshift mounting extension of the rear fork end of the bicycle frame via a horizontal shaft 6 and through-hole 11 (corresponding to second connecting structure 8b of the present application); the other end connects the rear derailleur via pins 20, 21 and corresponding pin holes (corresponding to first connecting structure 8a of the present application); the end of an adjusting screw 40 (corresponding to positioning structure 8c of the present application) abuts against a stop portion 101a on the gearshift mounting extension to position the rear derailleur relative to the rear fork end; and it can be seen from Figure 4 that the positions of the pins 20, 21 and the corresponding pin holes are below and behind the through-hole 11. Thus, Document 3 has already disclosed all technical features of claim 1, and they belong to the same technical field. Therefore, the technical solution claimed in claim 1 is not new relative to the prior art disclosed in Document 3 and does not comply with the novelty requirement of Article 22, paragraph 2 of the Patent Law."

In response to the second office action, Shimano Inc. further amended the claims and submitted a second statement of opinions. This amendment mainly further limited new claim 1 to more clearly describe the difference in installation methods between the present invention and the bicycle derailleur of Document 3, made textual changes to claim 2 and split it into a new dependent claim 4, and added new dependent claims 3 and 6. In the second statement of opinions, Shimano Inc. stated: "Document 3 is a prior U.S. patent of the same applicant as the present application, disclosing a bicycle rear derailleur, which also does not disclose a bracket body (8) as described in the present application. The 'base member 1' mentioned in Document 3 is actually a component of the four-bar linkage of the derailleur, one end of which is connected to the threaded hole 101b on the gearshift mounting extension of the rear fork end of the bicycle frame via a horizontal shaft 6 and through-hole 11. Therefore, this 'base member 1' is not equivalent to the 'bracket body 8' of the present application. It can be said that the derailleur disclosed in Document 3 is directly mounted on the gearshift mounting extension of the rear fork end of the bicycle frame. In contrast, the present invention discloses a bicycle rear derailleur bracket for connecting a rear derailleur (100) to a bicycle frame (50). Specifically, the rear derailleur has a bracket member (5), a support member (4) for supporting a chain guide (3), and a pair of connecting members (6, 7) for connecting the support member (4) and the bracket member (5). The present invention connects the bracket member (5) of the rear derailleur to one end of the bracket body (8) of the bracket, and then connects the other end of the bracket body (8) to the gearshift mounting extension (14) of the rear fork end (51) of the bicycle frame."

After this amendment, the patent application was granted, and the claims as amended for the second time are consistent with the claims in the granted patent text.

During the retrial of this court, Shimano Inc. submitted two new pieces of evidence: a receipt for patent fees from the State Intellectual Property Office (dated January 19, 2012) (Evidence 1) and a notarial certificate, (2011) Jing Zhong Xin Nei Jing Zheng Zi No. 6943 (Evidence 2). Evidence 1 was used to prove that the patent in question is still in force; Evidence 2 was used to prove that images of the accused infringing product appeared in a product brochure distributed by Richeng Company at the 2011 China Northern International Bicycle and Electric Vehicle Exhibition and that Richeng Company was still committing acts of infringement of the patent in question, and requested that this circumstance be considered in determining damages. Richeng Company had no objection to the authenticity of the above two pieces of evidence but disputed the evidentiary purpose of Evidence 2, arguing that this evidence could not achieve Shimano Inc.'s evidentiary purpose, as Richeng Company only offered to sell the accused infringing product and did not prove actual manufacturing or sales. For the above two pieces of evidence, this court certifies as follows: Regarding Evidence 1, Shimano Inc. provided the original of this evidence, and Richeng Company had no objection to its authenticity; this court accepts it. Regarding Evidence 2, this evidence is a notarial certificate produced by a notary public; Richeng Company had no objection to its authenticity, and it is relevant to this case; this court accepts it. In light of the above two pieces of evidence, this court finds the following facts: On March 31, 2011, agents ad litem of Beijing Puhua Law Firm, Liang Chenqi and Wang Xuefei, went to the Tianjin Meijiang Convention and Exhibition Center, located at the northwest corner of the intersection of Youyi South Road and the Outer Ring Road in Xiqing District, Tianjin. At the booth of Richeng Company, Booth No. 5B36, at the Eleventh China Northern International Bicycle and Electric Vehicle Exhibition, Wang Xuefei, as an ordinary visitor, took photographs of the booth and obtained a brochure marked "SUNRUN INDUSTRY&TRADE" from the booth. The notary public of Beijing Zhongxin Notary Office notarized the above process and issued the notarial certificate (2011) Jing Zhong Xin Nei Jing Zheng Zi No. 6943. Pages 32 and 33 of the Richeng Company brochure attached to the notarial certificate contain images of the accused infringing products in this case, the RD-HG-30A and RD-HG-40A bicycle rear derailleurs. As of now, the patent in question remains in force.

During the retrial of this court, Richeng Company filed a motion to suspend the proceedings in this case and submitted as evidence a notice of acceptance of an invalidation request from the Patent Reexamination Board, a patent invalidation request, and relevant prior art documents. It was found that Richeng Company had filed a request with the Patent Reexamination Board on January 9, 2012 to declare the patent in question invalid, and the request had been accepted. In the invalidation procedure, Richeng Company submitted three prior art documents: U.S. Patent No. 4,690,663 (Document 1), European Patent Publication EP 0,013,136 (Document 2), and U.S. Patent No. 4,612,004 (Document 3). The main grounds for invalidation were: independent claim 1 of the patent in question and claims 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6, which depend on claim 1, all lack essential technical features and do not comply with Article 21, paragraph 2 of the Implementing Regulations of the Patent Law; the patent in question does not comply with Article 33 of the Patent Law, as the amendments go beyond the original disclosure; the patent in question does not comply with Article 26, paragraph 4 of the Patent Law, as the claims are not supported by the description; claim 1 of the patent in question is a simple combination of technical features disclosed in the prior art and lacks inventiveness under Article 22, paragraph 3 of the Patent Law, and claims 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 also lack inventiveness.

During the proceedings of this court, Richeng Company also raised a prior art defense, claiming that its accused infringing product utilized prior art. The prior art claimed by Richeng Company included two types: first, Document 1 (U.S. Patent No. 4,690,663) submitted in the invalidation procedure combined with common general knowledge; second, a combination of Figure 2, Figure 6, and Figure 10 of the "Light Industry Standard of the People's Republic of China — Bicycle Derailleurs" (QB/T 1895-1993) and Figure 10 of the "Industry Standard of the People's Republic of China — Bicycle Industry Standard — Bicycle Frames" (QB1880-93).

This court holds that the infringing act in this case occurred before the implementation of the Patent Law amended in 2008 and should be governed by the Patent Law amended in 2000. In light of the reasons for retrial submitted by the applicant, the defense of the respondent, and the facts of this case, the issues in dispute between the parties are: whether the use environment features in claim 1 of the patent in question limit the scope of protection of the claim and the extent of such limitation; whether the accused infringing product in this case is necessarily used with the bicycle frame defined in claim 1 of the patent in question; whether the accused infringing product in this case falls within the scope of protection of the patent in question; whether the proceedings in this case should be suspended; whether the respondent's prior art defense is established; and the bearing of civil liability in this case.

(I) Whether the use environment features in claim 1 of the patent in question limit the scope of protection of the claim and the extent of such limitation

Use environment features refer to technical features in a claim that describe the background or conditions under which the invention is used. Regarding the limiting effect and extent of use environment features on the scope of protection of a claim, this court analyzes as follows:

First, regarding the limiting effect of use environment features on the scope of protection. Any technical feature written into a claim shall be understood as an indispensable necessary technical feature of the patented technical solution, which has a limiting effect on the scope of patent protection and must be considered when determining the scope of protection. Use environment features that have been written into a claim constitute necessary technical features of the claim and have a limiting effect on the scope of protection of the claim. The protection subject of the patent in this case is "a rear derailleur bracket for a bicycle," but Claim 1, while describing the structural features of the rear derailleur bracket, also defines the specific structures of the rear derailleur to which the bracket is connected and the bicycle frame. These features concerning the rear derailleur and bicycle frame to which the rear derailleur bracket is connected in fact define the background and conditions for the use of the rear derailleur bracket and constitute use environment features, which have a limiting effect on the rear derailleur bracket protected by Claim 1. The feature of the bicycle frame used by the rear derailleur bracket protected by Claim 1 is "the bicycle frame has a connecting structure (14a) formed on a derailleur mounting extension (14) of a rear fork end (51) of the bicycle frame" (hereinafter referred to as use environment feature 1). The feature of the rear derailleur used by the rear derailleur bracket protected by Claim 1 is "the rear derailleur has a bracket member (5), a support member (4) for supporting a chain guide device (3), and a pair of connecting members (6, 7) for connecting the support member (4) and the bracket member (5)" (hereinafter referred to as use environment feature 2). Together with other features of Claim 1, they form a complete technical solution and jointly define the scope of protection of Claim 1.

Second, regarding the degree of limitation of use environment features on the scope of protection. The degree of limitation here refers to the extent of the limiting effect of the use environment feature on the scope of the claim, specifically whether the protected subject object limited by this type of use environment feature must be used in such a use environment or may be used in such a use environment. The degree of limitation of a use environment feature on the scope of protection needs to be specifically determined on a case-by-case basis. Generally, a use environment feature should be understood to require that the protected subject object may be used in such a use environment, but does not require that the protected subject object must be used in such a use environment.
